replacement.title: Repair warranty: code still says six extra months; official guidance differs

replacement.summary: The consumer code still gives a six-month extension after repair, where the EU amendment requires twelve. Official guidance is inconsistent: one government page describes twelve months already, while another says national transposition is still underway.
replacement.euChange: The repair directive adds a once-only twelve-month extension of the seller's liability period where repair brings goods into conformity. Its amendment applies to sales contracts concluded on or after 31 July 2026.
replacement.nationalGap: Article L217-13 still specifies a six-month extension; the live code dated 26 October 2026 retains its 2021 version. Article L217-3 retains a two-year liability period. Service Public’s September news item says transposition is underway and contrasts six months with the forthcoming year, but its consumer guide, verified in August, already describes twelve months.
replacement.nationalLaw: Consumer Code Articles L217-3 and L217-13; Civil Code Article 1648.
replacement.provisions: Directive 2024/1799 Article 16(2), inserting Directive 2019/771 Article 10(2a) and (5a); Articles 21 and 22; French Consumer Code L217-3 and L217-13.
replacement.consequence: Possibly. The inspected code still specifies six extra months after repair, compared with twelve in the EU amendment. One official consumer guide already describes twelve months, while another says the national change is pending. This conflicting guidance leaves the practical position uncertain; no refused extension or consumer loss has been established.
replacement.resolution: We found no enacted twelve-month replacement in the current official code or in a bounded search of later legislation. The government itself acknowledges that the extension awaits transposition.
replacement.caveat: Focus this comparison on contracts concluded after 31 July 2026 and goods actually repaired. The EU alternative for systems without a fixed liability period does not obviously fit France's express two-year period. Repair downtime, replacement rights, commercial guarantees and the separate hidden-defects remedy can provide additional protection; this is not a claim that every repaired product has only thirty months of coverage. The practical effect of consistent interpretation requires legal assessment. Official guidance is inconsistent: Service Public guide F11094 describes a twelve-month extension, while news item A19033 still describes six months pending transposition. This is a statutory-wording lead, not a definitive account of every consumer’s enforceable rights or current practice.

replacement.title: Energy sharing: collective rules still require a legal entity
replacement.statusLabel: Collective route still requires a legal entity
replacement.statusDetail: Equivalent private-agreement route needs legal review
replacement.evidenceLabel: Live current statutory and regulatory provisions checked
replacement.summary: France’s framework for collective self-consumption still links participants through a legal entity. We found no equivalent route without one. Ordinary authorised direct electricity sales are already possible, which is an important qualification.
replacement.nationalGap: Energy Code L315-2 requires producers and consumers in ordinary and extended collective self-consumption operations to be linked within a legal person. D315-9, rewritten in June 2026 and effective 1 July, still requires that person to contract with the distribution-system operator. The current framework therefore retains the organisational requirement rather than expressly providing the private-agreement alternative. The 2026 allocation reforms do not remove it.
replacement.nationalLaw: Energy Code L315-2 and D315-9; direct-sale alternative L333-1(I)(2).
replacement.provisions: Amending Article 2(5); revised Article 15a(2), (4); Article 3(1). National L315-2, D315-9, L333-1.
replacement.consequence: Possibly. The collective self-consumption route inspected still requires an organising legal entity. France also permits authorised direct private sales; whether another route provides equivalent sharing rights, including metered deduction and the small-household supplier exemption, needs legal assessment. No refused project or quantified harm has been established.
replacement.resolution: We read the current provisions L315-2 and D315-9 on 25 October 2026. Searches of later legislation and official sources found no separate sharing framework without a legal entity. The Commission’s September 2026 procedure concerns incomplete implementation of energy sharing and supplier choice more broadly; it does not prove this specific difference.
replacement.caveat: L333-1(I)(2) permits direct private sales where the producer has supplier authorisation or delegates the obligations to an authorised third party. Such a sale is not automatically equivalent to energy sharing with metered deduction and the small-household supplier exemption in Article 15a(4). Existing collective projects remain possible; geographic limits, balancing responsibilities and charges may lawfully apply. This is a qualified framework comparison requiring legal assessment, not an adjudicated infringement.

replacement.summary: Portugal’s new safeguard expressly suspends interruption orders for the disputed invoice only. Whether it also covers termination and disputes not about billing needs legal review.
replacement.euChange: New Article 28a(2) protects against termination or disconnection on complained-of grounds.
replacement.nationalGap: Article 185(5)–(7) ties the stay to the disputed invoice, with continuation and repeat-complaint rules. It does not expressly add termination protection or a general stay for non-billing disputes. The quality regulation likewise addresses billing errors.
replacement.nationalLaw: Decree-Law 15/2022 Article 185(5)–(7), as amended by Decree-Law 130/2026; RQS Article 64; RRC Articles 78–88.
replacement.provisions: Amending Article 2(9); revised Article 28a(2); Article 3(1). National Article 185.
replacement.consequence: Possibly. The new express stay concerns the disputed electricity invoice, while the EU safeguard also addresses termination and other complained-of grounds. Existing Portuguese termination limits and complaint, arbitration and court remedies may supply protection. Their combined equivalence and any practical shortfall remain unestablished.
replacement.resolution: The amendment took effect on 28 August 2026 and is in the current consolidated text. We found no later general safeguard of the same kind in the rules we checked.
replacement.caveat: The rule concerns the grounds under complaint, not an unconditional ban on every interruption during a dispute. Payment obligations continue and appropriate anti-abuse procedures are permitted. Portuguese law already limits supplier termination, requires notice, provides complaints and mandatory consumer arbitration, and allows judicial protection. The complaint branch of Article 185(5) must be interpreted in context; its final disputed-invoice phrase, rather than the grammar of the billing-dispute modifier alone, underpins this comparison. Directive-consistent interpretation or another applicable remedy may protect individual customers. No safety-related interruption is presented as prohibited, and no practical enforcement failure is alleged.

replacement.statusLabel: Current statutory period · EU rights require individual assessment

replacement.summary: Belgium’s statute still specifies 90 days after work authorisation ends, without an express longer period for longer-standing permit holders. EU protection and other residence grounds may affect an individual’s right to stay.
replacement.nationalGap: Article 61/25-2(5) ends residence automatically 90 days after work authorisation ends. It contains no longer-period exception based on permit-holding duration. Flanders’ guidance likewise describes three months.
replacement.nationalLaw: Law of 15 December 1980, Article 61/25-2(5); Cooperation Agreement of 2 February 2018, Article 36(2).
replacement.consequence: Yes, on paper. The statute has no express longer period for people who have held the permit for more than two years, as the EU rule has. Individuals can invoke sufficiently precise EU rights directly, and no unlawful individual withdrawal or removal has been established.
replacement.resolution: The current official database (Justel) keeps the rule; we found no later remedy.
replacement.caveat: This concerns ordinary single permits with validity remaining and time-limited regional work authorisation; separate Blue Card, seasonal, intra-corporate and unrestricted-status rules are excluded. Notification and sufficient-resources conditions may apply. Individuals may invoke sufficiently precise EU rights against public authorities. Article 61/25-4 preserves more favourable EU rules in the residence section; it is not itself a textual replacement of the earlier procedural section. Other residence grounds, pending applications, individual circumstances and judicial protection require assessment. A 90-day national sentence does not establish that EU protection is unavailable.
replacement.review: A separate researcher checked the authentic EU provision and deadline, live Justel wording and amendment dates, current Flanders guidance, later-measure searches and the EU-rights saving route. The comparison passed as a qualified statutory/practice wording lead, with no finding about an actual removal.
replacement.recognitionNote: Decker Law’s 18 October 2026 analysis juxtaposes the national 90-day rule and the revised longer EU protection. The article is currently indexed but its live page redirects to maintenance; it is used only for prior recognition.
